analysis.one_liner: Creates a bill of rights for student loan borrowers, limiting servicer fees, credit reporting errors, and forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the Student Borrower Protections Act 32-26 in December 2019, but the bill never received a vote by the full House and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written a "bill of rights" for people repaying student loans, covering both federal loans and private ones. It would require lenders and loan servicers to send clear monthly statements, give 45 days' notice before a loan is transferred, limit late fees, investigate billing errors on a deadline, connect struggling borrowers with repayment specialists, and stop using forced arbitration clauses that block borrowers from suing. It also would set federal standards for how student loan information is reported to credit bureaus and require colleges to certify private student loans and tell students about cheaper federal aid first. The House Financial Services Committee approved it 32-26 in December 2019, but it never got a vote by the full House and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 45 million Americans with student debt would gain a set of enforceable servicing rights: clear monthly statements showing how payments are split between principal and interest, 45-day notice and a 90-day no-penalty window when a loan is sold or transferred to a new servicer, limits on late fees (no fee within 15 days of the due date, capped at 4% of the past-due amount, never charged more than once per late payment), a right to have billing errors investigated within 30 business days with no negative credit reporting during the dispute, repayment specialists for borrowers who fall behind, specially trained liaisons for servicemembers and veterans (including a ban on reporting combat-zone borrowers as delinquent), free access to their full loan history and original loan documents, and a ban on forced arbitration and class-action waivers in student loan contracts. [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student loan borrowers, federal and private

how_it_helps.text: Borrowers would get detailed monthly billing statements showing the interest rate, principal balance, how each payment was split between principal and interest, any fees itemized, and how to file a complaint with the CFPB or the Education Department.

When a loan is sold or transferred to a new servicer, the old and new servicers would both have to notify the borrower 45 days in advance, and the borrower could not be charged late fees or hit with negative credit reporting for payments caught in the transition.

Borrowers could send a qualified written request about their loan and get acknowledgment within 5 business days and a full response within 30 business days, with no negative credit reporting, late fees, or interest capitalization while the dispute is pending.

Servicers would have to designate repayment specialists to contact any borrower who is 30 or more days delinquent or says they are struggling, review eligibility for alternative repayment plans and discharges, and tell borrowers about those options before pushing forbearance.

Servicemembers and veterans would get a specially trained liaison at each servicer, and a loan could not be charged off or reported delinquent while the borrower is on active duty in a designated combat zone.
Forced arbitration clauses and class-action waivers in student loan contracts would be unenforceable, so borrowers could take disputes to court or join class actions.

Private lenders would have to obtain a certification from the student's college stating the cost of attendance and remaining financial need, and the college would have to tell the student about federal aid options and the right to cancel a private loan before the loan is made.

analysis.who_pays: Student loan servicers and private student lenders would bear the compliance costs: new billing statement requirements, 45-day transfer notices, dispute-response deadlines, staffing of repayment specialist and servicemember liaison units with call-hour minimums, loss of late-fee revenue, exposure to lawsuits, and the end of forced arbitration clauses. Colleges would take on new duties to certify private loans and disclose federal aid options before a private loan is made. [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Student loan servicers and private lenders

drawbacks.text: Servicers and private lenders would face substantial compliance costs — new statements, staffing, call centers, and dispute systems — and some of those costs could be passed back to borrowers through higher interest rates or fees.

The college certification requirement inserts institutions of higher education into the private loan process and, under the bill's 15-day rule, a lender could proceed with a loan if the college simply fails to respond in time, which could allow loans to be made without real review.

Most provisions regulate how loans are serviced rather than what they cost: the bill sets no cap on interest rates and provides no debt relief, so borrowers in unaffordable loans would get better treatment but not a smaller balance.

The bill relies heavily on CFPB rulemaking — model forms, allocation rules, credit reporting standards — so the real-world protections would depend on how rigorously the bureau writes and enforces the rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver meaningful, enforceable protections to tens of millions of borrowers who currently face opaque statements, surprise servicer transfers, fee stacking, and arbitration clauses — problems the record of servicer misconduct has repeatedly documented. The main costs fall on servicers and private lenders, some of which could be passed to borrowers as higher prices, and the bill does nothing about the underlying size of student debt or interest rates. On balance, the borrower protections are substantial and the cost is a genuine but secondary compliance burden.

outcome.mechanism: The Financial Services Committee approved it 32-26 in December 2019, but House leadership never brought it to the floor for a vote, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 4, 2019, and referred to the Financial Services Committee and the Education and Labor Committee.
The Financial Services Committee held markup sessions on December 10 and 11, 2019, and voted 32-26 to order the bill reported with amendments.
The committee action was the last entry in the bill's history; no report was filed and the House never voted on it before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan servicers and private lenders are better off: they continue operating under the existing rules, keep late-fee revenue, and retain arbitration clauses. Borrowers got nothing from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student loan servicers and private lenders

sides.party_line_note: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill on a 32-26 vote in a Democratic-majority committee, a split close to party lines, but the bill never reached a full House vote.

industries.industry: Federal student loan servicers and debt collectors
industries.note: The bill imposes detailed servicing rules: payment-allocation methods that benefit the borrower, late-fee limits, mandatory dispute timelines, call-hour minimums, and a ban on paying staff based on collections volume. These directly cut into fee revenue and compliance flexibility that servicers currently enjoy.

Private lenders would have to obtain a certification from the student's college before making a loan, disclose federal aid options to the borrower, send quarterly statements during school, and accept a ban on forced arbitration and class-action waivers in their contracts.

The CFPB would write rules governing how student loan information is furnished to credit bureaus, covering servicer transfers, loan duration, and forbearance, with the CFPB empowered to take enforcement action against violators.

Colleges would be required to certify private loans and disclose federal aid options before a student signs one, adding administrative work; the disclosure duty also positions institutions as advisors in the borrowing process.
